title: Platform Engineer Solution Framing and Conversation Guide
author: Priya Rao
body:
Overview:

This guide is written for sales engineers and account executives engaging platform engineering teams at target accounts. It distills a technical conversation framework, sample messaging tailored to platform engineers, a compact competitive brief, pricing scenarios with unit economics, a short demo checklist, and a focused security & compliance FAQ. Use this as the canonical playbook when the buyer persona is an infrastructure/platform team evaluating inference runtime and deployment integration.

Key objectives:
- Rapidly establish credibility with platform/infra engineers by speaking to integration, observability, and operational guarantees.
- Translate Redwood product capabilities into measurable engineering outcomes (latency SLOs, throughput predictability, operational cost).
- Give clear next steps that match typical platform procurement (tech eval -> pilot -> dedicated capacity -> private deployment).

Audience and conversation map:
- Primary: Platform / Infrastructure Engineers, ML Platform leads.
- Secondary: ML Engineers (model owners), Security/Compliance.
- Conversation hooks: predictable throughput, autoscaling behavior, network & private connectivity options, auditability and key management, rollback and safe deploys.

Messaging pillars (short scripts for calls and demos):
1) Predictable serving economics
- Opening line: "We help platform teams make inference cost predictable and debuggable — not just cheaper models. Think: tokens and latency you can forecast."
- Evidence to cite: autoscaling policies, dedicated GPU pools, and per-route token-level cost breakdowns in Redwood Console.

2) Unified runtime across deployment modes
- Opening line: "Same API, same telemetry, and same rollout primitives whether you run hosted, dedicated, or in your VPC. That reduces integration and long-term operational debt."
- Evidence to cite: model pinning, rollout policies, and local dev -> staging -> prod parity.

3) Reliability with graceful degradation
- Opening line: "We prioritize keeping features online — automatic fallback to compatible model variants or regions when capacity is constrained."
- Evidence to cite: smart routing, multi-region failover, and SLA-backed Dedicated tiers.

Technical value statements and data points to use:
- Typical p95 token latency for short (<512-token) generations on our Dedicated config: 70–140 ms depending on model family and quantization profile.
- SLA: 99.9% availability (Dedicated) with 30-minute incident notification commitments on enterprise contracts.
- Cost example (ballpark): $45–$140 per million generation tokens before discounts depending on model family and quantization. Use explicit quoting in live deals.
- Autoscaling: fast vertical scale up for burst capacity, horizontal scaling with per-GPU placement policies.

Competitive brief (concise matrix you can read in 90 seconds):
- Key comparators: CloudOEM endpoints, OpenRuntime self-host stacks, ModelEndpointCo managed endpoints.
- Differentiators to emphasize: unified runtime across hosted/dedicated/private, built-in rollout and fallback policies, token-level cost and latency telemetry, engineering-first SDKs and tracing hooks, pre-curated quantization and batching recommendations via Redwood Optimize.

Competitive talking points by scenario:
1) If competitor sells lower sticker price: "Ask about observability and unit economics — their low price often assumes fixed batch sizes or no KV cache, meaning unpredictable latency when traffic spikes."
2) If competitor emphasizes open-source freedom: "We support self-hosted/custom infra but pair it with an operational control plane, audit logs, and customer-managed keys to reduce integration work and ongoing ops load."
3) If competitor sells a single-tenant appliance: "Confirm how they handle model rollouts and graceful fallback across regions — appliance often equals single failure domain unless they offer multi-region orchestration."

Sample objection responses (platform-focused):
- Objection: "We already have a Kubernetes-based inference stack."
  Response: "Great — most customers run a mix. We integrate with existing K8s clusters for on-prem variants, and our control plane can manage model pinning/rollouts and observability so your SREs don’t have to build and maintain tracing and cost telemetry."
- Objection: "We can’t send customer data to hosted providers."
  Response: "We offer Redwood Private (VPC/on-prem) with customer-managed keys and audit logs; for sensitive workflows we can scope a pilot to an air-gapped or VPC-restricted environment."

Pricing guidance and pilot economics (playbook with example scenarios):
- Structure recommendations: Start with a 6–8 week pilot using Redwood Hosted + Dedicated trial credits to prove SLOs. For pilots targeting production latency and throughput, provision a small Dedicated pool (1–2 GPUs) and add a short horizon of burst capacity.

- Pricing scenario table (example numbers for discussion only):
  - Small inference pilot: 1 GPU equivalent, estimated 50M tokens/month -> Est. list cost $2,500–$6,000/month (includes burst & storage).
  - Mid-scale production (reserved): 4 GPU dedicated pool, 800M tokens/month -> Est. list cost $30k–$60k/month depending on model family and quantization.
  - Private deployment license: platform fee (one-time) + annual support. Typical enterprise private deals are structured as: platform fee $X (negotiated) + per-GPU / per-month support and optional managed services.

- How to present discounts: anchor on predictable unit economics rather than headline token price. Offer committed-volume discounts and milestone credits tied to SLO attainment during pilot.

Demo checklist (30–45 minute technical demo for platform engineers):
1) Authentication & network integration (10 min)
   - Show API key management and customer KMS integration.
   - Demonstrate VPC peering example sequence and firewall rules.
2) Observability & tracing (10 min)
   - Walk Redwood Console per-route latency and token-cost dashboard.
   - Show a trace from request -> kernel selection -> response, point out KV cache hit-rate metric.
3) Rollouts & safety (10 min)
   - Create a canary rollout: pin a model version, run traffic split, show automatic fallback after simulated failure.
4) Performance and scaling (10 min)
   - Show batch size and latency tradeoff via simple workload toggle.
   - Run a short throughput test and display autoscaling behavior.

Sample API snippet to use in demos (showing structured call + tool-calling placeholder):
{
  "model": "redwood-xlarge-v1",
  "input": "Summarize the incident, include impacted services and remediation actions.",
  "max_tokens": 256,
  "trace_id": "demo-12345"
}

Case study vignette (one-paragraph):
- FinOps PlatformCo reduced inference costs by 38% while improving median request latency by 22% after migrating a tiered serving strategy to Redwood Dedicated. Key enablers were prefix caching for common prompts, model quantization profiles recommended by Redwood Optimize, and per-route autoscaling to avoid sustained overprovisioning.

Security & compliance FAQ (platform team focus):
Q: Can we manage keys and ensure logs never leave our VPC?
A: Yes. Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS, HSM integrations, and optional local log ingestion with forwarding disabled. Logs can be configured to persist only in customer-managed S3/GCS buckets or on-prem storage.

Q: How are audit trails formatted and retained?
A: Audit logs include request metadata, user/principal, model version, and response hash. Retention is configurable per-customer; typical defaults are 90 days with enterprise retention add-ons available to 7+ years. Logs are exportable in JSON or newline-delimited JSON.

Q: What network topologies are supported for private deployments?
A: VPC peering, private link, on-prem direct connect, and air-gapped cluster installation are supported. See deployment guide for port lists and recommended MTU/MTLS settings.

Q: How do you handle data residency and regional sovereignty?
A: Customers can pin workloads to regions; Redwood control plane supports region-aware routing and model residency policies. Private on-prem installs give full local residency.

Q: What compliance frameworks do you support?
A: We maintain SOC 2 Type II readiness and provide evidence packages; for high regulatory needs we offer dedicated compliance engagements and support for customer-provided attestations.

Putting it into a deal motion (play-by-play):
1) Discovery (0–2 weeks): technical intake call with platform lead to gather SLOs, peak QPS, data residency, and compliance needs.
2) Proposal & pilot design (week 2): propose pilot scope (traffic shape, model variants, metrics).
3) Pilot (6–8 weeks): provision trial Dedicated pool, run integration and telemetry checks, iterate on quantization/batching.
4) Evaluation & procurement (weeks 10–14): share pilot report with cost/latency delta and propose committed capacity.
5) Rollout (post-sign): migrate traffic, establish runbooks and oncall rotations.

Ownership and next steps:
- Recommended internal owner for this play: Sales Engineering (primary) with Platform Solutions (secondary).
- Offer: provide a pre-built pilot template and a short technical RACI that lists required customer roles (network engineer, security lead, SRE) and Redwood contacts (SE, Solutions Architect, Customer Success).

Appendix: Useful snippets and links to bring to calls:
- Example firewall port list: 443 (API), 853 (mTLS internal) -- confirm ports per deployment guide.
- Recommended SLOs to align on: p95 latency target, request success rate (>= 99.5%), and cost per 1M tokens target.
- Quick checklist to qualify for Dedicated: predictable traffic shape, latency-sensitive features, and need for data isolation.

Document maintenance:

End of document.
